audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Since your group projects make up forty percent of your final grade this semester, I'd like to spend a few minutes on how to work together effectively. First, at your very first meeting, write a team agreement. Decide how often you'll meet, how quickly people should reply to messages, and what happens if someone misses a deadline. Groups that do this usually have far fewer conflicts later on.

Second, divide the work by skills, not just by sections of the report. For example, one person might be good at finding sources, while another is better at designing slides. And rotate the role of coordinator every two weeks, so that no single person ends up doing all the organizing.

Finally, remember that at the end of the semester, each of you will complete an anonymous peer evaluation. Your individual grade can go up or down by as much as ten percent, depending on what your teammates report. If problems come up, please come to my office hours early. Don't wait until the week before the presentation.

passage: For many university students, the words "group project" bring to mind one familiar problem: the free rider, a teammate who does little work but receives the same grade as everyone else. In a Student Association survey last spring, 68 percent of the 1,200 respondents said they had worked with at least one free rider, and nearly half said the experience made them dislike group assignments.

This semester, the Center for Teaching and Learning is testing a possible solution. Twelve courses across four colleges are using an online platform called TeamTrack. Students use it to divide tasks, set personal deadlines, and upload drafts. The platform automatically records who completed each task and when, and instructors can view a summary of each member's activity at any time.

Supporters say the tool makes contributions visible. "Before, I had to rely on students telling me who did what," said Professor Huang Ya-wen, who teaches business communication. "Now I can see the process, not just the final product." Several students also said they felt more motivated knowing their work was being recorded.

However, not everyone is convinced. Some students worry that the platform measures activity rather than quality. "Someone can upload ten small files and look busy, while the person who writes the most important section only uploads once," said Chen Po-han, a sociology junior. Others have raised privacy concerns and want to know who else can see the data.

The center will collect feedback from students and teachers at the end of the semester. If the results are positive, TeamTrack could be offered to all courses by next fall. In the meantime, the center recommends that groups continue to use written team agreements and regular peer evaluations.
